question: What defines an adverse drug reaction compared to a normal drug action?

options.A: It disappears without altering the dose.
options.B: It only happens when a patient overdoses.
options.C: It is harmful and occurs at normal doses.
options.D: It is a planned therapeutic outcome.

explanation: Adverse drug reactions are harmful and unexpected responses that happen even when the drug is taken correctly at standard doses. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why must a nurse separate a routine side effect from an adverse drug reaction?

options.A: Adverse reactions often demand a change in therapy.
options.B: Routine side effects are always fatal to patients.
options.C: Adverse reactions only occur in pediatric wards.
options.D: Side effects never require nursing documentation.

explanation: Unlike mild side effects that patients tolerate, true adverse reactions usually force the clinician to stop or switch the medication. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: What characterizes a Type A adverse drug reaction?

options.A: It is caused by sudden immune allergies.
options.B: It never occurs with standard drug doses.
options.C: It is completely unrelated to pharmacology.

explanation: Type A reactions stem from the primary pharmacological effect of the medication and happen more often when doses are high. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: An unexpected allergic rash develops after a standard dose of an antibiotic. What reaction type is this?
explanation: Allergic reactions do not depend on the drug dose and happen unpredictably in susceptible individuals, fitting the Type B category. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which patient group is most vulnerable to drug accumulation and adverse reactions?

options.A: Athletes with high muscle mass ratios
options.B: Healthy young adults with fast metabolism
options.D: Older adults with decreased renal clearance

explanation: Declining kidney and liver function in older adults slows down drug elimination, making them prone to toxic build-up. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient with severe liver cirrhosis is prescribed a drug cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism. What is the main risk?

options.A: The drug will immediately cure the liver disease.
options.B: The drug will accumulate and cause toxicity.
options.C: The drug will pass through without any effect.
options.D: The patient will develop an instant antibiotic allergy.

explanation: Liver damage stops proper drug breakdown, causing high blood levels of the medication and severe adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why must nurses ask about herbal remedies when assessing for adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Patients usually take herbs instead of modern medicines.
options.B: Herbs can interact with prescription drugs to cause toxicity.
options.C: Herbal products replace the need for hospital laboratory tests.
options.D: Traditional herbs never cause any adverse side effects.

explanation: Many patients combine orthodox drugs with local herbs, which can alter drug metabolism and trigger unexpected adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient develops a sudden skin rash two hours after receiving a new intravenous antibiotic. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Stop the infusion and notify the prescriber.
options.B: Document the rash and wait for the next shift.
options.C: Give a standard dose of oral paracetamol.
options.D: Increase the fluid flow rate to dilute the drug.

explanation: Stopping the suspected drug immediately prevents further exposure and reduces the severity of an adverse reaction. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary management step when a severe adverse drug reaction occurs?

options.A: Double the dose to build patient immunity.
options.B: Switch the patient to a traditional herbal remedy.
options.D: Wait for laboratory confirmation before acting.

explanation: Removing the source of the reaction stops further harm and allows stabilization to begin. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: How does medication reconciliation at hospital admission prevent adverse drug reactions?

options.A: It eliminates the need for daily vital sign checks.
options.B: It guarantees the patient will take drugs on time.
options.C: It catches duplicate therapies and potential drug clashes.
options.D: It lowers the financial cost of purchasing drugs.

explanation: Comparing a patient's home medications with new hospital orders prevents dangerous interactions and accidental overdoses. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which Nigerian agency is responsible for regulating drugs and monitoring adverse reactions?
explanation: The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control handles drug safety surveillance and pharmacovigilance in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of submitting a yellow form to the national pharmacovigilance center?

options.A: To apply for nursing license renewal
options.B: To report suspected adverse drug reactions
options.C: To request free drug supplies for the ward
options.D: To register a new pharmacy business

explanation: The yellow form is the standard tool used by health workers to report unexpected or severe drug reactions to regulatory authorities. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)
